Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 1 - Exponents & Radicals for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

For a≠0 and integers m,n:

  1. am·an=am+n
  2. aman=am−n
  3. (am)n=amn
  4. (ab)m=ambm
  5. (ab)m=ambm
  6. a0=1
  7. a−m=1am

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Examples

  • x3·x5=x8
  • y7y2=y5
  • (2x)3=8x3
  • x−4=1x4
  • Substitute the value of the base and apply exponent rules.
  • Negative bases behave differently depending on exponent parity.

Examples

content:
Unit 2 - Percent — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 2 - Percent for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

A percent is a ratio out of 100.

Percent=PartWhole×100
  • 50% = 50100=12
  • 25% = 25100=14
  • 200% = 200100=2

Formula

Percent Change=New−OriginalOriginal×100%
  • Positive → increase
  • Negative → decrease
  • Linear growth: constant addition per step
    Example: salary increases $2000 each year → y = 2000t + P
  • Exponential growth: constant multiplication per step
    Example: bacteria doubles every hour → y=P(2t)

1) Convert: (a) 0.2 to percent, (b) 150% to decimal. 2) Find percent change: 60 → 45. 3) Simple interest: $800 at 6% for 2 years. 4) Compound interest: $500 at 8% annually for 2 years. 5) Linear growth: population starts at 1000, grows by 50 per year. Write equation. 6) Exponential decay: medicine amount starts at 200 mg, halves each hour. Write equation. 7) Identify association:

  • Number of hours worked vs. income.
  • Hours of TV watched vs. GPA.

1) (a) 0.2=20% (b) 150%=1.5
2) 45−6060×100=−25% (decrease)
3) I=800(0.06)(2)=96
4) A=500(1.08)2=583.20
5) y=1000+50t
6) y=200(0.5)t
7) Positive: hours worked vs. income. Negative: TV hours vs. GPA.

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Examples
1. Price from 40to\50:

50−4040×100=25% increase
  1. Price from 80to\60:
60−8080×100=−25% decrease

Simple Interest

I=Prt
  • P = principal
  • r = rate (decimal)
  • t = time

Example: 1000at5I = 1000(0.05)(3)=150$

Compound Interest

A=P(1+rn)nt
  • A = total
  • P = principal
  • r = annual rate (decimal)
  • n = times compounded per year
  • t = time in years

Example: $1000 at 5% compounded annually for 3 years

A=1000(1.05)3=1157.63

Example 1
40% of students are girls. If there are 200 students, how many are girls?

0.40×200=80

Example 2
An item is discounted 20%, then taxed 5%. If original price is $100:

  • After discount: 100(0.8)=80
  • After tax: 80(1.05)=84

Linear growth/decay equation:

y=y0+kt
  • k>0: growth
  • k<0: decay

Example
A tank loses 5 liters per hour, starting with 200:

y=200−5t

General formula:

y=y0(1±r)t
  • + for growth
  • − for decay

Example
Car worth $20,000 depreciates 10% per year:

y=20000(0.9)t
  • Positive association: as x increases, y tends to increase.
  • Negative association: as x increases, y tends to decrease.

Examples

  • Speed vs. travel time → negative

Key idea

A linear equation has the general form:

ax+b=c

Next idea

Steps:

  1. Move variable terms to one side.
  2. Move constants to the other.
  3. Divide by the coefficient of x.

Example

Example

5x+2=3x+8⇒5x−3x=8−2⇒2x=6⇒x=3

SAT Tip: Always combine like terms before solving.

Example

x3+x6=5

Multiply through by the least common multiple (LCM) of the denominators:

6(x3+x6)=6(5)⇒2x+x=30⇒3x=30⇒x=10

A quadratic equation has the form:

ax2+bx+c=0

Unit 4 - Rates — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 4 - Rates for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

A rate compares two different quantities with different units.

Rate=Quantity AQuantity B
  • Always include units - many traps involve mismatched units.
  • For combined rates, add rates, not times.
  • For ratios in word problems, set up proportions.
  • Convert early to avoid mistakes (miles → feet, hours → minutes).

1) A runner covers 10 km in 50 minutes. What is her speed in km/h?
2) Convert 5 feet to inches
3) A car travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours. Find speed in mph
4) A faucet fills a tub in 15 minutes, another in 20 minutes. How long together?
5) A cyclist rides 12 miles in 40 minutes. Find unit rate in miles per hour.

1) 1050=0.2 km/min → 0.2×60=12 km/h
2) 5 ft·12 in1 ft=60 in
3) r=1502.5=60 mph
4) Rates: 115+120=760 tubs/min. Time = 607≈8.57 min
5) 1240=0.3 miles/min → 0.3×60=18 mph

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Examples - Speed = distancetime

  • Density = massvolume
  • Price per item = costnumber of items

A unit rate expresses the rate per 1 unit.

Examples - 180 miles in 3 hours → 1803=60 miles/hour

  • 12for4poundsofapples→\dfrac{12}{4} = 3$ dollars/pound

A conversion factor is a fraction equal to 1, used to change units.

Common examples - 1 hour=60 minutes

  • 1 inch=2.54 cm
  • 1 mile=5280 ft

Example
Convert 5 hours to minutes:

5 hr·60 min1 hr=300 min Distance=Rate×Time
  • d=rt

Rates: A=14, B=16. Combined = 14+16=512

Unit 5 - Expressions — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 5 - Expressions for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  • Like terms have the same variable raised to the same power.
  • Only their coefficients can be added or subtracted.
  • Always factor before canceling terms in fractions.
  • Look for special products: (a+b)2, (a−b)2, a2−b2.
  • Simplify step by step; avoid canceling across addition.
  • Expressions with radicals or fractions often simplify after factoring.

1) Simplify: 4x+7−3x+2
2) Expand: (x+4)(x−2)
3) Factor: x2+9x+20
4) Simplify: 34+56
5) Simplify: x2+6xx

1) x+9
2) x2+2x−8
3) (x+5)(x+4)
4) 912+1012=1912
5) x(x+6)x=x+6 (for x≠0)

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Examples - 3x+5x=8x

  • 7y−2y=5y
  • 2x2+3x−x2+4=(2x2−x2)+3x+4=x2+3x+4

Expansion

Use distributive property:

a(b+c)=ab+ac

Examples - (x+2)(x+3)=x2+5x+6

  • (2x−5)(3x+4)=6x2−7x−20

Factoring

Reverse of expansion.

  • Take out common factor.
  • Use special patterns:
  1. Difference of squares:
a2−b2=(a−b)(a+b)
  1. Perfect square trinomials:
a2+2ab+b2=(a+b)2 a2−2ab+b2=(a−b)2

Examples - x2+7x+10=(x+5)(x+2)

  • 9x2−25=(3x−5)(3x+5)

Adding/Subtracting

Must have common denominator.

ab+cd=ad+bcbd

Example

23+56=46+56=96=32

Multiplying

Multiply numerator and denominator directly.

ab·cd=acbd

Dividing

Multiply by reciprocal.

abÃ·cd=ab·dc

Splitting Fractions

Distribute denominator:

a+bc=ac+bc

Example

x+63=x3+2

content:
Unit 6 - Manipulating & Solving Equations — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 6 - Manipulating & Solving Equations for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  1. Cancelling incorrectly

    • Wrong: x+5x=1+5=6
    • Correct: x+5x=1+5x

  2. Losing solutions when multiplying/dividing by a variable

    • If you multiply or divide by x, always check x≠0.

  3. Forgetting to distribute negatives

    • −(x+3)=−x−3, not −x+3

  4. Square root mistake

    • x2=|x|, not x

Inverse operations

  • Addition ↔ Subtraction
  • Multiplication ↔ Division
  • Squaring ↔ Square root

Example
Solve 3x+7=16

3x=9⇒x=3

Balancing equations

What you do to one side, do to the other.

Distribute and Combine

  • Expand parentheses and combine like terms.

Example
Solve 2(x+3)−(x−5)=12

2x+6−x+5=12⇒x+11=12⇒x=1

Fractions

  • Multiply through by least common denominator (LCD).

Example
Solve x3+25=1
Multiply both sides by 15:

5x+6=15⇒x=95

Decimals

  • Multiply through by powers of 10 to clear decimals.

Example
Solve 0.2x+0.5=1.3
Multiply through by 10:

2x+5=13⇒x=4
  • Always simplify before solving.
  • Eliminate fractions and decimals early.
  • Plug solution back to check (some SAT questions have “extraneous solutions”).
  • Watch for absolute values, square roots, and restrictions.

2) Solve: 2(x−3)+4=10
3) Solve: 3x4+2=5
4) Solve: 0.1x+0.2=0.5

Unit 7 - More Equation Solving Strategies — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 7 - More Equation Solving Strategies for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

Useful when equations are polynomials or involve unknown coefficients.

Example 1
Suppose (ax+b)(x+2)=2x2+7x+6
Expand LHS: ax2+(2a+b)x+2b
Match coefficients with RHS:

  • a=2
  • 2a+b=7⇒4+b=7⇒b=3
  • 2b=6 (checks out)

So a=2,b=3.

For equations with fractions, multiply both sides by the least common denominator (LCD).

Example 2
Solve x2+34=5
LCD = 4. Multiply through:

2x+3=20⇒2x=17⇒x=172

Example 3
Solve 2x+3x+1=1
LCD = x(x+1). Multiply through:

2(x+1)+3x=x(x+1) 2x+2+3x=x2+x⇒x2−4x−2=0

Solve quadratic:

x=4±16+82=4±242=2±6
  • Always check for restrictions when clearing denominators (denominators ≠0).
  • Matching coefficients often appears in SAT questions with polynomial identities.
  • After clearing denominators, check for extraneous solutions by plugging back.

1) Solve for a and b: (ax+b)(x+1)=3x2+7x+2
2) Solve: x3+56=4
3) Solve: 1x+1x+2=34
4) Solve: 2y−1y+3=1

1) Expand LHS: ax2+(a+b)x+b. Match with RHS 3x2+7x+2:

  • a=3
  • a+b=7⇒3+b=7⇒b=4
  • b=2 conflict! → no solution.

2) Multiply through by 6: 2x+5=24⇒2x=19⇒x=192

3) LCD = x(x+2): (x+2)+x=34(x2+2x)
Simplify: 2x+2=34(x2+2x)
Multiply by 4: 8x+8=3x2+6x
3x2−2x−8=0

Solve: x=2±4+966=2±106
→ x=2 or x=−43

4) LCD = y(y+3): 2(y+3)−y=y(y+3)
2y+6−y=y2+3y

y+6=y2+3y y2+2y−6=0

Solve: y=−2±4+242=−2±282=−2±272
→ y=−1±7

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 8 - Systems of Equations for SAT Math preparation.
content:
Unit 8 - Systems of Equations — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 8 - Systems of Equations for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  • Solve one equation for one variable, then substitute into the other.

Example 1
Solve:

y=2x+3 3x+y=12

Substitute y=2x+3:

3x+(2x+3)=12⇒5x+3=12⇒5x=9⇒x=95


Then y=2(95)+3=185+155=335.

Solution: (95,335).

  • Add or subtract equations to eliminate one variable.

Example 2
Solve:

2x+3y=12 4x−3y=6

Add equations: 6x=18⇒x=3
Substitute: 2(3)+3y=12⇒6+3y=12⇒y=2
Solution: (3,2).

  • No solution (inconsistent): parallel lines with different intercepts
    Example: y=2x+3, y=2x−4.

  • Infinite solutions (dependent): equations are multiples of each other
    Example: 2x+4y=6, x+2y=3.

Example 3
A movie ticket costs $12 for adults and $8 for children. If 5 tickets cost $52, how many adult and child tickets?

Let a = adults, c = children.

a+c=5 12a+8c=52

Multiply first eqn by 8: 8a+8c=40. Subtract from second: 4a=12⇒a=3
Then c=2.

Solution: 3 adult, 2 child tickets.

Sometimes 3 equations with 3 unknowns.

Example 4
Solve:

x+y+z=6 2x−y+z=4 x+2y−z=5

From first: z=6−x−y
Substitute into second: 2x−y+(6−x−y)=4⇒x−2y+6=4⇒x−2y=−2⇒x=2y−2.

Sub into third: (2y−2)+2y−(6−(2y−2)−y)=5
Simplify: 2y−2+2y−(6−2y+2−y)=5.

4y−2−(8−3y)=5 4y−2−8+3y=5⇒7y−10=5⇒7y=15⇒y=157

Then x=2(157)−2=307−147=167.

z=6−167−157=42−317=117

Solution: (167,157,117).

  • Each equation = line.
  • Solution = intersection point(s).
  • No intersection → no solution.
  • Same line → infinite solutions.

Example 5

y=2x+1

and y=−x+4


Graph: they intersect at (1,3).

  • Always check the form: sometimes substitution is easier, sometimes elimination.
  • Be alert for “trick” systems (no solution or infinite).
  • Graphs can help visualize.
  • For word problems: define variables clearly, then set up equations.

1) Solve:

x+2y=7 3x−y=5

2) Solve:

2x+3y=10 4x+6y=12

3) Tickets to a play cost 5forstudentsand\12 for adults. If 10 tickets total $81, how many of each type?

4) Solve:

x+y=4 x−y=2

5) Solve the 3-variable system:

x+2y+z=9 2x−y+z=4 x−y+2z=8

1) From first: x=7−2y. Substitute: 3(7−2y)−y=5⇒21−6y−y=5⇒−7y=−16⇒y=167. Then x=7−327=177. Solution: (177,167).

2) Second eqn is multiple of first but different constant → no solution.

3) s+a=10, 5s+12a=81. Multiply first by 5: 5s+5a=50. Subtract: 7a=31⇒a=317 (not integer). On SAT, maybe trick - check wording.

4) Add equations: 2x=6⇒x=3. Then 3+y=4⇒y=1. Solution: (3,1).

5) From first: x=9−2y−z. Substitute into second: 2(9−2y−z)−y+z=4⇒18−4y−2z−y+z=4⇒−5y−z=−14⇒5y+z=14. Call this (A)
Also substitute into third: (9−2y−z)−y+2z=8⇒9−3y+z=8⇒−3y+z=−1⇒3y−z=1. Call this (B)
Add (A)+(B): 8y=15⇒y=158. Then 3(158)−z=1⇒458−z=1⇒z=378. Then x=9−2(158)−378=72−30−378=58
Solution: (58,158,378).

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 9 - Inequalities for SAT Math preparation.
content:
Unit 9 - Inequalities — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 9 - Inequalities for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

Rules are similar to solving equations, with one key difference:

  • When multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number, the inequality sign flips.

Example 1
Solve: 3x−7<11

3x<18⇒x<6

Example 2
Solve: −2x+5≥9

−2x≥4⇒x≤−2

Translate carefully from words to math.

Example 3
A concert ticket costs $40. You have at most $250. How many tickets can you buy?

40x≤250⇒x≤6.25

So maximum whole tickets = 6.

Example 4
A test requires at least 70 points to pass. You currently have 42 points out of 60. How many of the remaining 40 points must you get?

Let x = points you score on last part.

42+x≥70⇒x≥28

So you must earn at least 28 points.

  • For one-variable inequalities:
  • x<3 → open circle at 3, shade left.

  • x≥−2 → closed circle at -2, shade right.

  • For two-variable inequalities:

  • Example: y≤2x+1 → graph line y=2x+1. Shade below because of ≤.
  • Use dashed line for < or >; solid line for ≤ or ≥.

Example 5
Graph solution set of:

y>−x+2

Line: y=−x+2, slope −1, intercept 2. Dashed line. Shade region above.

The solution is the overlap region of all shaded areas.

Example 6
Graph and solve:

y≥x+1 y<−2x+4

The solution region is the intersection of the two shaded half-planes.

  • Always flip the inequality when multiplying/dividing by negative.
  • Check boundary points (does equality hold?).
  • For word problems, highlight key phrases like “at most,” “at least,” “no more than.”
  • Graph shading is common on SAT - test with a sample point like (0,0).

1) Solve: 5x+2>17
2) Solve: −3x+7≤1
3) A taxi charges 4perrideplus\2 per mile. You have at most $30. How many miles can you ride?
4) Solve and graph: y≤12x+3
5) System of inequalities:

y>2x−1,y≤−x+4

1) 5x+2>17⇒5x>15⇒x>3.

2) −3x+7≤1⇒−3x≤−6⇒x≥2.

3) Cost equation: 4+2m≤30⇒2m≤26⇒m≤13. So up to 13 miles.

4) Line: y=12x+3, slope 12, intercept 3. Solid line (since ≤). Shade below.

5) Graph both: y>2x−1 (above dashed line), y≤−x+4 (below solid line). Solution = overlap region.

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1) 5x+2>17⇒5x>15⇒x>3.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 10 - Word Problems for SAT Math preparation.
content:
Unit 10 - Word Problems — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 10 - Word Problems for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

Example 1
A number increased by 7 is 20. Find the number.

Let x = the number.

x+7=20⇒x=13

Example 2
A rectangle has length 3 more than twice its width. If the perimeter is 42, find dimensions.

Let width = w, length = 2w+3.

2w+2(2w+3)=42⇒2w+4w+6=42⇒6w=36⇒w=6

Then l=2(6)+3=15
Rectangle: 6×15.

Distance = rate × time.

Example 3
A car travels 60 miles in the same time a train travels 100 miles. If the train is twice as fast, find car’s speed.

Let r = car speed. Train speed = 2r
Time = distance/rate.

60r=1002r⇒60r=50r

Contradiction → no solution. Check: maybe train is not exactly twice but “20 mph faster.”

Revised Problem
Car: r, Train: r+20, Times equal.

60r=100r+20

Cross-multiply: 60(r+20)=100r⇒60r+1200=100r⇒40r=1200⇒r=30
Car = 30 mph, Train = 50 mph.

Work rate = 1 / (time to finish).

Example 4
Alice can paint a room in 4 hours, Bob in 6 hours. How long together?

Rates: Alice = 1/4, Bob = 1/6. Together = 1/4+1/6=5/12
So time = 1/(5/12)=12/5=2.4 hours.

Example 5
A 20-liter solution is 25% acid. How much water to add to make it 10% acid?

Acid = 0.25(20)=5 liters
Final solution: 20+x liters, still 5 acid.

520+x=0.10⇒5=0.1(20+x)⇒5=2+0.1x⇒0.1x=3⇒x=30

Add 30 liters water.

Example 6
Find three consecutive integers whose sum is 96.

Let numbers = n,n+1,n+2.

n+(n+1)+(n+2)=96⇒3n+3=96⇒3n=93⇒n=31

Numbers: 31, 32, 33.

  • Define variables before writing equations.
  • Watch out for “at least,” “at most” (inequalities).
  • Always answer in the context of the problem (no raw variables).
  • Plug answer choices back in if stuck (backsolving).

1) A number decreased by 8 is 15. What is the number?
2) A rectangle has width w and length 3w. If area = 75, find w
3) A plane flies 600 miles in the same time a car drives 200 miles. If plane speed is 4 times car speed, find speeds
4) Two workers can finish a job in 5 hours together. If one works twice as fast as the other, how long alone for each?
5) A 40-liter mixture is 30% sugar. How much pure sugar to add to make it 50% sugar?

1) x−8=15⇒x=23.

2) w(3w)=75⇒3w2=75⇒w2=25⇒w=5.

3) Car = r, Plane = 4r. 600/(4r)=200/r⇒150/r=200/r. Contradiction → recheck wording. Likely: “Plane is 300 mph faster.”
Try: 600/(r+300)=200/r. Cross multiply: 600r=200(r+300)⇒600r=200r+60,000⇒400r=60,000⇒r=150. Car = 150 mph, Plane = 450 mph.

4) Let slow = r, fast = 2r. Together rate = 3r. Time = 1/(3r)=5⇒3r=1/5⇒r=1/15. So slow = 15 hrs, fast = 7.5 hrs.

5) Sugar initially = 0.3(40)=12. Add x sugar → total sugar = 12+x, total volume = 40+x
Equation: (12+x)/(40+x)=0.5⇒12+x=0.5(40+x)=20+0.5x.

0.5x−x=12−20=−8⇒−0.5x=−8⇒x=16


Add 16 liters sugar.

content:
Unit 11 - Lines — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 11 - Lines for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  • Slope (m): measures steepness.
m=riserun=y2−y1x2−x1
  • y-intercept (b): point where line crosses y-axis.

Equation form:

y=mx+b

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example 1
Find slope and intercept of line through (2,3) and (4,7).

m=7−34−2=42=2

Equation: y=2x+b. Plug (2,3): 3=2(2)+b⇒3=4+b⇒b=−1
Final: y=2x−1.

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1) Find slope and intercept of line through (0,4) and (2,10). 2) Write equation of line with slope 5 through (1,−3). 3) Find intersection of y=3x+1 and y=−2x+6.

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

Slope-Intercept Form

y=mx+b

Point-Slope Form

y−y1=m(x−x1)

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2
Equation of line through (1,2) with slope −3:

y−2=−3(x−1)⇒y=−3x+5

Solve system of equations.

Example 3
Find intersection of y=2x+1 and y=−x+4.

Set equal:

2x+1=−x+4⇒3x=3⇒x=1

Then y=2(1)+1=3
Intersection = (1,3).

  • Parallel lines: same slope, different intercepts.
  • Perpendicular lines: slopes multiply to −1 (negative reciprocals).

Example 4
Find equation of line parallel to y=3x+2 through (0,5).

Slope = 3. Equation: y=3x+5.

Example 5
Find equation of line perpendicular to y=12x−1 through (2,0).

Slope = −1(12)=−2
Equation: y−0=−2(x−2)⇒y=−2x+4.

  • Horizontal: y=c (slope = 0).
  • Vertical: x=c (slope undefined).

Example 6
Equation of line through (3,−2) and parallel to y=−2:
Answer: y=−2.

Example 7
Equation of line through (4,5) and parallel to x=1:
Answer: x=4.

  • Memorize slope formulas.
  • Parallel → same m.
  • Perpendicular → m1·m2=−1.
  • Watch out for vertical/horizontal lines.
  • For intersections, substitution is often faster than graphing.

1) Find slope and intercept of line through (0,4) and (2,10)
2) Write equation of line with slope 5 through (1,−3)
3) Find intersection of y=3x+1 and y=−2x+6
4) Write equation of line parallel to y=−4x+7 through (2,1)
5) Write equation of line perpendicular to y=2x−5 through (−1,2).

1) m=(10−4)/(2−0)=6/2=3. Equation: y=3x+4.

2) Point-slope: y+3=5(x−1)⇒y=5x−8.

3) 3x+1=−2x+6⇒5x=5⇒x=1,y=4. Intersection (1,4).

4) Parallel slope −4. Equation: y−1=−4(x−2)⇒y=−4x+9.

5) Perpendicular slope −12. Equation: y−2=−12(x+1)⇒y=−12x+32.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 12 - Interpreting Linear Models for SAT Math preparation.
content:
Unit 12 - Interpreting Linear Models — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 12 - Interpreting Linear Models for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  • Slope is the change in y per unit change in x.
  • Interpreted as a rate.

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example 1
A taxi company charges according to the equation:

Cost=2.5x+4

where x = miles traveled.

  • Slope = 2.5 → cost increases by $2.50 per mile.
  • Intercept = 4 → flat starting fee = $4.

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1) A cell phone plan costs C=40+0.1m, where m = number of minutes. Interpret slope and intercept.

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

  • Intercept is the value of y when x=0.
  • Often represents initial condition.

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2
Temperature T=70−2t, where t = hours after noon.

  • Intercept = 70 → temperature at noon = 70°F.
  • Slope = -2 → temperature drops 2°F each hour.

You can use the equation to predict values.

Example 3
A company’s revenue is modeled by:

R=5000+200t

where t = months.

  • After 6 months:
R=5000+200(6)=6200

So revenue = $6200.

  • Models may not apply for all x.
  • Negative values may be meaningless (e.g., negative time, negative price).
  • Always check context.

Example 4
If h=100−5t gives height of rocket (t= seconds), then at t=30:

h=100−150=−50

Negative height is meaningless → model only valid for small t.

On the SAT:

  • A line of best fit is given.
  • You may be asked to interpret slope/intercept.
  • Or check if a point fits the model.

Example 5
Scatterplot shows relation between study hours (x) and test score (y). Line of best fit:

y=50+5x
  • Intercept = 50 → baseline score with 0 study = 50.
  • Slope = 5 → each study hour adds 5 points.
  • Identify units for slope/intercept.
  • Watch for unrealistic predictions.
  • If a graph/table is shown, pick two points to compute slope.
  • Double-check whether the model describes growth or decline.

1) A cell phone plan costs C=40+0.1m, where m = number of minutes. Interpret slope and intercept.

2) A car’s value is modeled as V=20,000−1200y, where y = years since purchase. What does slope mean?

3) A fitness app predicts weight loss with W=180−2t, where t = weeks. Find weight after 5 weeks.

4) The line of best fit for data is y=30+4x. Interpret slope in context.

5) A model predicts y=100−15x. For x=10, what is y? Is this prediction reasonable?

1) Intercept = 40 → fixed monthly fee 40.Slope=0.1→eachminuteadds\0.10.

2) Slope = -1200 → car loses $1200 value each year.

3) W=180−2(5)=170. After 5 weeks, weight = 170 lbs.

4) Slope = 4 → each increase of 1 unit in x raises y by 4.

5) y=100−15(10)=100−150=−50. Prediction meaningless (negative). Model not valid for large x.

More practice

Keep going—aim for accuracy first, then speed.

content:
Unit 13 - Functions — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 13 - Functions for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  • Each x has only one y.
  • You cannot have two outputs for the same input.

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example 1
Is this a function?

  • (1,2),(2,3),(3,4) → Yes (every input unique).
  • (1,2),(1,3),(2,4) → No (input 1 has two outputs).

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1) Is y=x a function? Why or why not? 2) For h(x)=5x+2, where is it undefined? 3) If f(x)=3x−4 and g(x)=x2+1, find (g∘f)(2).

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

  • Division by zero is not allowed.
  • Square roots of negatives are not real.
  • Logarithms of nonpositive numbers are undefined.

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2

f(x)=1x−3

is undefined at x=3

Example 3

g(x)=x−5

is undefined if x<5

If f(x) and g(x) are functions, then:

(f∘g)(x)=f(g(x))

Example 4
If f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x2, find (f∘g)(3).

(f∘g)(3)=f(g(3))=f(9)=2(9)+1=19

Solve f(x)=k for x.

Example 5
If f(x)=x2−4, solve f(x)=5.

x2−4=5⇒x2=9⇒x=±3
  • Vertical Line Test: If a vertical line crosses graph more than once → not a function.

Example 6

  • y=x2 → function (parabola passes test).
  • Circle x2+y2=1 → not a function (fails vertical line test).
  • Watch for undefined values.
  • Composition is a common SAT trick.
  • Always check if graphs pass vertical line test.
  • Solutions to f(x)=k mean x-values where graph crosses y=k.

1) Is y=x a function? Why or why not?
2) For h(x)=5x+2, where is it undefined?
3) If f(x)=3x−4 and g(x)=x2+1, find (g∘f)(2)
4) Solve f(x)=x2+2x when f(x)=8
5) Does the graph of a sideways parabola x=y2 represent a function?

1) Yes, y=x is a function since each input has only one output (though domain is x≥0).

2) Denominator =0 at x=−2, so undefined there.

3) (g∘f)(2)=g(f(2))=g(2)=(22+1)=5 where f(2)=3(2)−4=2. So g(2)=5.

4) x2+2x=8⇒x2+2x−8=0⇒(x+4)(x−2)=0⇒x=−4,2.

5) No, x=y2 fails vertical line test (two y for each x>0).

Keep going—aim for accuracy first, then speed.

content:
Unit 14 - Quadratics — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 14 - Quadratics for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

The roots/solutions of a quadratic are the x-values where y=0
Methods:

  1. Factoring
    Example: x2−5x+6=0
(x−2)(x−3)=0⇒x=2,3
  1. Quadratic Formula
    For ax2+bx+c=0:
x=−b±b2−4ac2a
  1. Completing the Square (see below).

Transform quadratic into vertex form.

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example 1
Solve x2+6x+5=0 by completing the square.

x2+6x+5=(x2+6x+9)−9+5=(x+3)2−4

Set =0:

(x+3)2=4⇒x=−3±2

So x=−1,−5.

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1) Solve x2−7x+12=0. 2) Solve 2x2+3x−5=0 using quadratic formula. 3) Find vertex of y=x2+4x−1.

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

A parabola’s vertex is given by:

x=−b2a,y=f(−b2a)

Vertex form:

y=a(x−h)2+k

where (h,k) = vertex.

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2

y=x2−4x+1

Vertex: x=42=2.

y=(2)2−4(2)+1=4−8+1=−3


Vertex = (2,−3).

The discriminant is inside quadratic formula:

Δ=b2−4ac
  • Δ>0 → 2 real roots
  • Δ=0 → 1 real root (double root)
  • Δ<0 → no real roots (complex roots)

Example 3

x2+2x+5=0

, Δ=22−4(1)(5)=4−20=−16<0

→ no real solutions.

Quadratics model motion, area, profit, etc.

Example 4
Height of ball: h=−16t2+32t+48 (feet).

  • Vertex gives maximum height.
t=−b2a=−322(−16)=1 h=−16(1)2+32(1)+48=64


Max height = 64 ft at t=1 sec.

  • Always check if factoring is quick.
  • Memorize quadratic formula.
  • Discriminant saves time for “how many solutions” questions.
  • Parabolas open upward if a>0, downward if a<0.

1) Solve x2−7x+12=0
2) Solve 2x2+3x−5=0 using quadratic formula
3) Find vertex of y=x2+4x−1
4) Determine number of real roots of x2+6x+10=0
5) A ball’s height is h=−5t2+20t+30. Find maximum height.

1) Factor: (x−3)(x−4)=0⇒x=3,4.

2) a=2,b=3,c=−5:

x=−3±32−4(2)(−5)2(2)=−3±494 x=−3±74⇒x=1,−52

3) x=−42=−2, y=(−2)2+4(−2)−1=4−8−1=−5. Vertex (−2,−5).

4) Δ=62−4(1)(10)=36−40=−4<0 → no real roots.

5) Vertex: t=−202(−5)=2.

h=−5(2)2+20(2)+30=−20+40+30=50


Max height = 50.

Keep going—aim for accuracy first, then speed.

content:
Unit 15 - Synthetic Division — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 15 - Synthetic Division for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

Steps: 1. Write down coefficients of dividend (fill in 0 for missing terms)
2. Write c from (x−c)
3. Bring down the first coefficient
4. Multiply by c, add to next coefficient, repeat.

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example 1
Divide 2x3+3x2−5x+6 by x−2.

Set up:

223−564141827924

Quotient: 2x2+7x+9, remainder 24
So:

2x3+3x2−5x+6x−2=2x2+7x+9+24x−2

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1) Divide x3+4x2−7x+2 by x−3. 2) Divide 2x3−9x2+7x+6 by x−2. 3) Use the remainder theorem: find remainder of f(x)=x4−5x3+2 when divided by x+1.

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

If remainder = 0, the divisor is a factor.

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2
Divide x3−6x2+11x−6 by x−1.

Set up:

11−611−61−561−560

Quotient: x2−5x+6, remainder 0
So (x−1) is a factor.

For f(x) divided by (x−c), the remainder is simply f(c).

Example 3

f(x)=x3+2x2−3x+1

. Find remainder when divided by x−2

Compute f(2)=23+2(22)−3(2)+1=8+8−6+1=11
So remainder = 11.

  • Use remainder theorem to save time.
  • If f(c)=0, then (x−c) is a factor.
  • Synthetic division only works for divisors of form (x−c), not x2+...

2) Divide 2x3−9x2+7x+6 by x−2
3) Use the remainder theorem: find remainder of f(x)=x4−5x3+2 when divided by x+1
4) Factor x3−4x2+x+6 completely using synthetic division
5) If f(x)=2x3+5x2−3x+1, is (x−1) a factor?

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 17 - Absolute Value for SAT Math preparation.
content:
Unit 17 - Absolute Value — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 17 - Absolute Value for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  1. |a|≥0 (always nonnegative).
  2. |−a|=|a|.
  3. |ab|=|a||b|.
  4. |ab|=|a||b|,b≠0.

Unit 18 - Angles — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 18 - Angles for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

In a triangle, the exterior angle is equal to the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.

Exterior Angle=Remote Interior Angle 1+Remote Interior Angle 2

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example 1
In a triangle, one exterior angle is 120∘. If one remote interior angle is 40∘, the other is:

120∘−40∘=80∘

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1) In a triangle, one angle is 50∘ and another is 60∘. Find the exterior angle adjacent to the third angle. 2) Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. If one angle is 75∘, find its alternate interior angle. 3) Find the sum of interior angles of a decagon.

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

When a transversal cuts two parallel lines:

  • Corresponding angles are equal.
  • Alternate interior angles are equal.
  • Same-side interior angles are supplementary.

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2
If one angle is 70∘, then the corresponding angle is also 70∘.

Interior Angle Sum

For an n-sided polygon:

Sum of interior angles=(n−2)×180∘

Each Interior Angle (regular polygon)

(n−2)×180∘n

Each Exterior Angle (regular polygon)

360∘n

Example 3
A hexagon (n=6):

  • Interior angle sum =(6−2)×180=720∘
  • Each interior angle =720/6=120∘
  • Complementary angles: sum =90∘
  • Supplementary angles: sum =180∘
  • Vertical angles: equal

Example 4
If two supplementary angles are in ratio 2:7, find them.

2x+7x=180⇒9x=180⇒x=20

Angles = 40∘,140∘

  • Always check for parallel lines → look for equal angles.
  • For polygons, memorize (n−2)×180∘.
  • Exterior angle theorem is very common.
  • Watch out for “trick” wording with supplements/complements.

4) (8−2)×180/8=6×180/8=108∘.

5) x+2x=90⇒3x=90⇒x=30.

A right triangle has one 90∘ angle

a2+b2=c2

where c is the hypotenuse.

a1a2=b1b2=c1c2

If △ABC~△DEF, and AB=4, BC=6, EF=9, find DE.

So DE=AB·32=4·32=6.

180∘=π radians

Conversions:

Convert 120∘ to radians:

120∘·π180=2π3

Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 20 - Circles for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  • Circumference:
C=2πr=πd
  • Area:
A=πr2

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example 1
If r=7, then:

C=14π,A=49π

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1) Find the circumference of a circle with r=10. 2) Find the area of a circle with diameter 12. 3) In a circle of radius 5, find the length of an arc subtended by 72∘.

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

Arc length is a portion of the circumference:

s=θ360∘·2πr

(or s=θr if θ in radians).

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2
Find the arc length of a 90∘ arc in a circle of radius 4.

s=90360·2π(4)=2π

Sector area is a portion of the total area:

Asector=θ360∘·πr2

(or Asector=12r2θ if θ in radians).

Example 3
Find the area of a 60∘ sector with r=6:

A=60360·π(36)=6π
  • Central angle: vertex at the circle’s center, equals arc measure.
  • Inscribed angle: vertex on the circle, equals half the arc it intercepts.

Example 4
If arc AB=80∘, then:

  • Central angle =80∘
  • Inscribed angle =40∘

General form:

(x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2

where (h,k) is the center and r the radius.

Example 5
Equation of circle centered at (3,−2) with r=5:

(x−3)2+(y+2)2=25
  • Inscribed angle = half arc is very common.
  • For arc/sector problems, always check if θ is in degrees or radians.
  • If you see x2+y2 terms, think “equation of a circle.”
  • Don’t forget diameter =2r when needed.

content:
Unit 22 - Reading Data — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 22 - Reading Data for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  • Tables: Organize data into rows and columns.
  • Bar Graphs: Compare discrete categories.
  • Line Graphs: Show trends over time.
  • Pie Charts: Show proportions of a whole.
  • Scatterplots: Show relationships between two variables.

Finding Totals

Add values across rows or columns.

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example 1
A table shows that 20 boys and 15 girls joined the math club.

Total=20+15=35

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1)

1) A bar graph shows sales: Monday 40, Tuesday 60, Wednesday 50.

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

  • What is the average daily sales?

Percentages

Convert part-to-whole into percent.

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2
In a survey, 30 students like soccer, 10 like basketball.

Soccer percent=3040×100=75%

Ratios

Express comparisons in simplest form.

Example 3
If a pie chart shows 120 students: 90 prefer cats, 30 prefer dogs.

Ratio cats:dogs=9030=3:1

Interpreting Trends

Look at increases/decreases in line graphs.

  • Rising line → positive trend.
  • Falling line → negative trend.
  • Flat line → no change.
  • Read axes carefully (units often trick students).
  • Watch for scales not starting at 0.
  • Double-check if a question asks for percent vs. raw number.
  • Ratios are part-to-part, percents are part-to-whole.

1) A bar graph shows sales: Monday 40, Tuesday 60, Wednesday 50.

  • What is the average daily sales?

2) A pie chart shows 200 students: 50 like math, 75 like science, rest like history.

  • What percent like history?

3) A line graph shows company revenue: Year 1 = 100k, Year 2 = 120k, Year 3 = 90k.

  • What is the overall percent change from Year 1 to Year 3?

4) A scatterplot shows a positive association.

  • What does this mean about the two variables?

1) Average = (40+60+50)/3=150/3=50.

2) History =200−(50+75)=75.

75200×100=37.5%

3) Change =90k−100k=−10k.

−10k100k×100=−10%

4) As one variable increases, the other tends to increase.

Unit 23 - Probability — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 23 - Probability for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

P(E)=Number of favorable outcomesTotal outcomes
  • 0≤P(E)≤1
  • P(certain event)=1
  • P(impossible event)=0

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example 1
A fair die is rolled. What is P(rolling a 4)?

P=16

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1)

1) A fair coin is flipped. Find P(Heads). 2) 2) A bag has 3 red, 2 blue marbles. Pick one at random. P(Blue)? 3) 3) Roll two dice. What’s P(sum = 7)?

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

P(not E)=1−P(E)

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2
Probability of rolling a 6 on a die is 16
Probability of not rolling a 6 is:

1−16=56

Events are independent if outcome of one does not affect the other.

P(A and B)=P(A)·P(B)

Example 3
Flip a coin and roll a die.

P(Heads and a 3)=12·16=112

Events that cannot both occur.

P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)

Example 4
Pick a card from a deck. P(Ace or King):

452+452=852=213

Use combinations or listing.

Example 5
From 5 students (A,B,C,D,E), 1 is chosen at random
Probability it’s A or B:

25
  • Decide if events are independent or mutually exclusive.
  • Watch for “at least one” → use complement rule.
  • In card/dice questions, always confirm total outcomes.
  • Reduce fractions!

3) Roll two dice. What’s P(sum = 7)?

3) Favorable outcomes: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) → 6 total
Total outcomes = 36.

P=636=16

4) Spades = 13, Hearts = 13.

5) 1−16=56.

Unit 24 - Statistics I — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 24 - Statistics I for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  • Mean (average):
Mean=Sum of valuesNumber of values
  • Median: Middle value when data is ordered.

  • If even number of values → average the two middle numbers.

  • Mode: The most frequent value.

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example 1
Data: [2,3,3,4,5]

  • Mean =(2+3+3+4+5)/5=17/5=3.4
  • Median =3
  • Mode =3

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1)

1) Find the mean of [4,6,8,10]. 2) 2) Data: [2,5,7,8,12]. What is the median? 3) 3) What is the mode of [1,2,2,3,4,4,4,5]?

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

  • Range:
Range=Max−Min
  • Standard Deviation (SD):
    A measure of how spread out data is
    Larger SD → more spread
    Smaller SD → values closer to the mean.

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2
Set A: [10,10,10,10] → SD = 0 (no spread)
Set B: [5,10,15] → larger spread, larger SD.

  • Histogram: Shows frequency of values in intervals (bins).
  • Dot Plot: Uses dots above a number line to show frequency.

SAT often asks:

  • Which interval is most common?
  • Approximate median/mean from the graph.

Example 3
The average of 4 test scores is 80. If three of them are 85, 75, 90, find the missing score.

85+75+90+x4=80⇒250+x=320⇒x=70
  • Always sort data before finding the median.
  • If one value is much larger/smaller → mean shifts, median less affected.
  • SD questions are usually relative (“which set has greater spread?”).
  • Carefully read graph axes.

5) A histogram shows most students scored between 70–80. What does this tell you about the mode?

2) Ordered set [2,5,7,8,12] → median =7.

3) Mode =4 (appears 3 times).

4) Range =22−5=17.

5) The mode is in the 70–80 interval.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 25 - Statistics II for SAT Math preparation.
content:
Unit 25 - Statistics II — Title & Goal
Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 25 - Statistics II for SAT Math preparation.

Key idea

Read the idea and scan the rules. Focus on how the symbols behave.

  • Random Sample: Every member has equal chance of being selected → most reliable.
  • Biased Sample: Favors certain members → unreliable.

Worked example

Follow the steps carefully, then try to reproduce them without looking.

Example
Surveying only basketball players to estimate average student height = biased
Surveying random students across school = better.

Quick practice

Try these on your own. Check your steps, not just the final answer.

1)

1) A school surveys only students in the honor society to estimate average study time. Is this sample biased?

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

Scatterplots often include a regression line.

  • Positive slope: As x increases, y tends to increase.
  • Negative slope: As x increases, y tends to decrease.
  • Closer points to line: Stronger correlation.

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example
If best-fit line is y^=2x+5, then for x=4:

y^=2(4)+5=13

Every estimate from a sample has some uncertainty.

  • Smaller sample size → larger margin of error.
  • Larger sample size → smaller margin of error.

Example
Poll shows 60% ± 3%. True population proportion is likely between 57% and 63%.

A confidence interval provides a range that likely contains the true population value.

  • A 95% confidence interval means if the survey were repeated many times, 95% of the intervals would contain the true value.

Example
A survey estimates average GPA = 3.2 with 95% CI (3.0,3.4)
Interpretation: The true GPA is likely between 3.0 and 3.4.

  • Correlation does not imply causation!
  • Randomized controlled experiments are most reliable.
  • Observational studies can show association but not cause.

Example
Data shows students who eat breakfast score higher
Conclusion: Eating breakfast is associated with higher scores, but may not be the cause (other factors like sleep could matter).

  • Look for wording like biased, random, representative.
  • Be careful: SAT may trick with causation vs. correlation.
  • For line of best fit → always use the equation given, not your own guess.
  • Interpret margin of error and confidence intervals correctly.

1) A school surveys only students in the honor society to estimate average study time. Is this sample biased?

2) A scatterplot shows a strong negative correlation. What does this mean?

3) A poll shows 48% support ± 4%. What is the interval of possible true support?

4) A best-fit line is y^=−3x+20. Predict y^ when x=5.

5) Researchers observe that students who text more tend to sleep less. Can they conclude texting causes less sleep?

1) Yes - it’s biased, since only honor students are surveyed.

2) As x increases, y tends to decrease.

3) Interval = (44%,52%).

4) y^=−3(5)+20=−15+20=5.

5) No - it only shows correlation, not causation.

1)

1) Find the volume of a rectangular box with dimensions 4×5×6.

Next idea

Build on the previous idea. Notice what changes and what stays the same.

  • Pyramid:
V=13(Base Area)(Height)
  • Cone:
V=13πr2h

Another example

Compare this approach to the previous one. What’s the same? What’s different?

Example 2
A cone with radius 4 and height 9:

V=13π(42)(9)=48π
V=43πr3

Example 3
A sphere with radius 5:

V=43π(53)=5003π

Sometimes shapes are combined or parts are removed
Strategy: Add or subtract volumes.

Example 4
A cylinder with r=3,h=10 is filled with a cone (r=3,h=10)
Volume difference = πr2h−13πr2h=23πr2h

=23π(9)(10)=60π
  • Always confirm if radius or diameter is given.
  • Watch units! SAT may ask in cubic centimeters, etc.
  • If asked about volume change, compare ratios instead of recalculating everything.
  • Example: If radius doubles, sphere’s volume increases by factor 23=8.

1) Find the volume of a rectangular box with dimensions 4×5×6.

2) A sphere has radius 7. Find its volume.

3) A cone has diameter 10 and height 12. Find its volume.

4) A cylinder has radius 5 and height 20. Find its volume.

5) If the radius of a sphere doubles, by what factor does its volume increase?

1) V=4×5×6=120.

2) V=43π(73)=13723π.

3) Radius = 5.

V=13π(52)(12)=100π

4) V=π(52)(20)=500π.

5) Volume increases by 23=8 times.

More practice

Keep going—aim for accuracy first, then speed.

Mixed practice set

These mix everything above. Time yourself and reflect on any mistakes.

description: Learn how parent functions are transformed through shifts, reflections, stretches, and compressions to create new graphs.
content:
Domain: Linear Functions and Equations
Unit 1: Parent Functions and Transformations

Definitions

  • Parent Function: The simplest function within a family (examples: linear, quadratic, absolute value, cubic, square root).
  • Transformation: An operation that moves or changes the graph’s position or shape, including shifts, reflections, stretches, and compressions.

Key Concepts

  • Translation (Shift):
    • Horizontal: f(x) → f(x - h) shifts right if h > 0, left if h < 0.
    • Vertical: f(x) → f(x) + k shifts up if k > 0, down if k < 0.
  • Reflection:
    • Across x-axis: f(x) → -f(x)
    • Across y-axis: f(x) → f(-x)
  • Stretch/Compression:
    • Vertical stretch by a: f(x) → a f(x)
    • Horizontal stretch by b: f(x) → f(bx)

Step-by-Step Procedure

  1. Start with the parent function’s graph.
  2. Apply horizontal shift: move right by h or left by -h.
  3. Apply horizontal/vertical stretch or compression as needed.
  4. Apply reflections across axes (if negative sign appears).
  5. Apply vertical shift: move up by k or down by -k.

Example 1

Graph f(x) = 2(x - 3)

  • Start: parent linear function f(x) = x.
  • Horizontal shift: right by 3 units (x → x-3).
  • Vertical stretch by 2: line becomes steeper.
  • y-intercept moves from (0, 0) to (3, 0).
  • Slope is now 2 (for each 1 unit increase in x, y increases by 2).

Example 2

Transform f(x) = |x| into g(x) = -|x+2| + 4

  • Start: parent absolute value function f(x) = |x|.
  • Replace x by x+2: shift left by 2 units.
  • Multiply by -1: reflect across x-axis.
  • Add 4: shift up by 4 units.
  • Vertex moves from (0, 0) to (-2, 4) and the 'V' opens downward.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Apply horizontal shifts before vertical ones.
  • In f(x - h), h: right if positive, left if negative.
  • In f(x) + k, k: up if positive, down if negative.
  • For reflections, watch whether the negative affects x or f(x).

Key Parent Functions Table

Function TypeParent FunctionGraph Summary
Linearf(x) = xStraight line through (0,0), slope 1
Quadraticf(x) = x^2Parabola, vertex at (0,0), opens up
Absolute Valuef(x) = |x|V-shape, vertex at (0,0), opens up
Cubicf(x) = x^3S-curve, passes through (0,0)
Square Rootf(x) = √xStarts at (0,0), increases slowly

unit: Unit 2: Transformations of Linear and Absolute Value Functions
description: Transform linear and absolute value functions using shifts, reflections, and stretches to sketch accurate graphs.
content:
Definitions

  • Linear Function: A function in the form f(x)=mx+b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept.
  • Absolute Value Function: A function of the form f(x)=a|x-h|+k with vertex at (h,k) and a "V" shaped graph.
  • Transformation: Changing the position or shape of a graph via shifts, stretches/compressions, or reflections.

Key Concepts

  • Linear Transformations:
    • Vertical and Horizontal Shifts: Move the line up/down (+k/-k) or left/right (x-h).
    • Reflection: Negative slope reflects over the x-axis.
    • Stretch/Compression: Changing the slope value (|m|) makes the line steeper or flatter.
  • Absolute Value Transformations:
    • Vertex shifts: h shifts horizontally, k shifts vertically.
    • Vertical Stretch/Compression: |a|>1 stretches, 0<|a|<1 compresses.
    • Reflection: If a<0, the "V" opens downward.

Step-by-Step Procedure

  • Identify the parent function (linear: y=x, absolute value: y=|x|).
  • Apply any horizontal or vertical shifts indicated by h and k.
  • Adjust for vertical stretch/compression and check for reflections (look at the coefficient in front).
  • Plot the new position of the key feature: the y-intercept for linear, the vertex for absolute value.
  • Draw the transformed graph.

Example 1

Transform f(x)=x into g(x)=-3(x+1)+2.

  • Starting function: f(x)=x.
  • Horizontal shift: left by 1 (x→x+1).
  • Vertical stretch by factor of 3 and reflect (multiply by -3): line is steeper and flipped.
  • Vertical shift: up by 2.
  • The new line has a slope of -3 and passes through (-1, 2).

Example 2

Graph f(x)=2|x-4|-3.

  • Parent function: y=|x|.
  • Horizontal shift: right by 4 units.
  • Vertical stretch: factor of 2 (makes "V" narrower).
  • Vertical shift: down by 3 units.
  • Vertex is now at (4, -3) and the "V" opens upward, narrower than parent.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • The sign inside the function affects horizontal moves (x-h is right, x+h is left).
  • Watch for negative signs outside the function—these cause reflections over the x-axis.
  • Double check both direction and magnitude of shifts before sketching.
  • Always plot the vertex for the absolute value graph first before drawing the arms.

Key Function Forms Table

FunctionParent FormTransformation ExampleGraph Effect
Linearf(x)=xg(x)=2(x-1)+3slope is 2, right 1, up 3
Absolute Valuef(x)=|x|h(x)=-|x+2|+4left 2, up 4, reflect

description: Model real-world situations using linear functions by interpreting and applying slope and intercepts.
content:
Definitions

  • Linear Model: An equation of the form y=mx+b that describes a straight-line relationship between two variables based on real-world data.
  • Rate of Change: The change in the dependent variable per one-unit increase in the independent variable; represented by the slope m in a linear model.
  • Y-Intercept: The point where the line crosses the y-axis (b in the equation).
  • Extrapolation: Predicting values outside the range of given data using the linear model.
  • Interpolation: Estimating values within the range of given data using the model.

Key Concepts

  • To model data with a linear function, determine if the relationship between the variables is approximately linear (the points should form or cluster around a straight line).
  • The slope (m) is calculated as y2-y1x2-x1 using two data points.
  • The y-intercept (b) is found by substituting a point and the slope into the equation y=mx+b and solving for b.
  • Use scatter plots to visually inspect if linear modeling is appropriate.
  • The line of best fit can be determined visually or calculated using regression (for large data sets).

Step-by-Step Procedure

  • Plot the data on a coordinate plane.
  • Select two points that best represent the trend (ideally widely spaced apart).
  • Calculate the slope (m).
  • Substitute one point and the slope into y=mx+b to find the y-intercept.
  • Write the linear equation.
  • Use the equation to make predictions or interpret real-life meaning.

Example 1

A cell phone plan costs $30 per month plus $0.10 per text message. Write a model for the total monthly cost C in terms of the number of messages n.

  • Slope (rate per message): 0.10.
  • Y-intercept (base charge): 30.
  • Model: C=0.10n+30.

Example 2

Given the data points (2, 7) and (6, 15), find the linear function that models the relationship.

  • Calculate slope: 15-76-2=84=2.
  • Use point (2, 7): 7=2·2+b implies b=3.
  • Model: y=2x+3.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Don't assume a linear model fits all data—always visualize with a scatter plot first.
  • Slope represents rate of change in context (e.g., cost per item, speed, etc.).
  • Be clear which variable is independent (usually x) and which is dependent (usually y).
  • Only extrapolate slightly beyond the data range; predictions far outside may not be reliable.

unit: Unit 4: Understanding Functions and Function Notation
description: Interpret functions and use function notation to describe and evaluate relationships.
content:
Definitions

  • Function: A relation that assigns exactly one output value for each input value.
  • Function Notation: If f(x) is a function, it represents the value of the function at input x.
  • Domain: The set of all possible input values (x-values) for the function.
  • Range: The set of all possible output values (f(x)-values) for the function.
  • Independent Variable: Typically x, the input for the function.
  • Dependent Variable: Typically f(x) or y, the output that depends on the input value.

Key Concepts

  • Function notation replaces y with f(x), clarifying what output arises from each input.
  • To evaluate a function, substitute the input value into every instance of x.
  • Functions can be represented as equations, tables, graphs, or word descriptions.
  • Check if a relation is a function: verify each input maps to only one output.

Step-by-Step Procedure

  • Given function notation f(x):
    1. Identify the formula for f(x). For example, f(x)=3x+5.
    2. Substitute the input value for x. Example: Find f(2).
    3. Calculate: f(2)=3⁢2+5=11.
  • Identify the domain and range by analyzing valid input values (avoid division by zero or square roots of negative numbers in real-valued functions).

Example 1

If g(x)=x2-4, find g(-3).

  • Substitute -3 for x: g(-3)=(-3)2-4=9-4=5

Example 2

Given h(x)=7x-8, evaluate h(0) and h(5).

  • h(0)=7⁢0-8=-8
  • h(5)=7⁢5-8=35-8=27

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Write function notation clearly: f(x), not just f or x.
  • Don’t confuse domain and range: domain is input, range is output.
  • A vertical line test on a graph checks if each input maps to one output (function).
  • Always test by plugging values in whenever unsure about output or notation.

unit: Unit 5: Graphing Linear Equations (Standard and Slope-Intercept Forms)
description: Graph linear equations from standard and slope-intercept forms and interpret slope and intercepts.
content:
Definitions

  • Slope-Intercept Form: y=mx+b where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept.
  • Standard Form: Ax+By=C where A, B, and C are constants.
  • Slope: The rate of change; rise over run, or y2-y1x2-x1.

Key Concepts

  • To graph a line in slope-intercept form, plot the y-intercept (b) and use the slope (m) to find another point: rise over run.
  • Standard form makes it easy to identify x- and y-intercepts by substituting 0 for y or x, respectively.
  • You can always convert standard form to slope-intercept form by solving for y.

Step-by-Step Procedure

  • For Slope-Intercept Form (y=mx+b):
    1. Plot the y-intercept (b).
    2. From that point, use the slope (m): up/down for numerator, right for denominator.
    3. Draw a straight line through your points.
  • For Standard Form (Ax+By=C):
    1. Find the x-intercept by setting y = 0: Ax=C. Solve for x.
    2. Find the y-intercept by setting x = 0: By=C. Solve for y.
    3. Plot these intercepts and draw the line through both points.

Example 1

Graph y=23x-1

  • Y-intercept: -1 (plot (0,-1))
  • Slope: 23 (up 2, right 3)
  • From the y-intercept, move up 2 units and right 3 units to plot another point.
  • Draw a line through the points.

Example 2

Graph 2x+3y=12 using intercepts

  • Set y = 0 for x-intercept: 2x=12 ⇒ x=6 (plot (6,0))
  • Set x = 0 for y-intercept: 3y=12 ⇒ y=4 (plot (0,4))
  • Plot both points and draw the line through them.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Watch for fractional slopes: move up/down and right/left accordingly.
  • Standard form is ideal for quickly finding intercepts; convert to slope-intercept to see the slope directly.
  • All points that satisfy the equation will be on the line you draw.

unit: Unit 6: Solving Linear Equations (Single and Multi-Step)
description: Solve single- and multi-step linear equations and justify each step using inverse operations.
content:
Definitions

  • Linear Equation: An equation that makes a straight line when graphed. It can be written in the form ax+b=c where a, b, and c are real numbers and a ≠ 0.
  • One-Step Equation: A linear equation that can be solved with a single operation (addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division).
  • Multi-Step Equation: A linear equation that requires two or more steps to solve, involving combining like terms and using more than one inverse operation.

Key Concepts

  • To solve for the variable, use inverse operations to isolate it on one side of the equation.
  • The properties of equality ensure that whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other.
  • Always simplify both sides if possible by distributing and combining like terms before solving.

Step-by-Step Procedure

  • Single-Step:
    1. If variable is added or subtracted: use addition or subtraction to isolate it. Ex: x+5=12 ⇒ subtract 5: x=7.
    2. If variable is multiplied or divided: use division or multiplication. Ex: 4x=20 ⇒ divide by 4: x=5.
  • Multi-Step:
    1. Distribute to remove parentheses if needed.
    2. Combine like terms on each side.
    3. Move variables to one side, constants to the other using addition/subtraction.
    4. Use multiplication/division to solve for the variable.
    5. Check your solution by substituting it back into the original equation.

Example 1 (One-Step)

Solve x-4=11

  • Add 4 to both sides: x=15

Example 2 (Multi-Step)

Solve 3(x-2)+4=19

  • Distribute: 3x-6+4=19
  • Combine like terms: 3x-2=19
  • Add 2 to both sides: 3x=21
  • Divide by 3: x=7

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always perform the same operation to both sides of the equation to keep them balanced.
  • Double-check signs when applying inverse operations.
  • For equations with no variable (e.g., 5=5), solution is all real numbers; for a false statement (3=8), there is no solution.
  • Substitute your answer back into the original equation to check your work.

unit: Unit 7: Solving Linear Systems (By Graphing, Substitution, Elimination)
description: Solve systems of linear equations using graphing, substitution, and elimination and interpret solutions.
content:
Definitions

  • System of Linear Equations: A set of two or more linear equations with the same variables.
  • Solution to a System: The values of variables that satisfy all equations simultaneously, often represented as ordered pairs.
  • Consistent System: A system with at least one solution.
  • Inconsistent System: A system with no solutions (parallel lines).
  • Dependent System: A system with infinitely many solutions (same line).

Key Methods

  • Graphing: Plot each equation; the intersection point is the solution. If lines are parallel (no intersection), no solution; if identical, infinite solutions.
  • Substitution: Solve one equation for one variable, substitute into the other, solve for the remaining variable, then back-substitute to find the first variable.
  • Elimination: Add or subtract equations to eliminate one variable; solve for the remaining variable and substitute back.

Step-by-Step Procedures

  • Graphing:
    1. Solve each equation for y (if needed).
    2. Plot key points (intercepts or points from slope).
    3. Draw lines and identify intersection points.
  • Substitution:
    1. Isolate one variable in one equation.
    2. Substitute this expression into the other equation.
    3. Solve for the remaining variable.
    4. Plug back to find the other variable.
  • Elimination:
    1. Arrange equations with variables and constants aligned.
    2. Multiply one or both equations to get opposite coefficients for one variable.
    3. Add or subtract equations to eliminate one variable.
    4. Solve for remaining variable.
    5. Substitute back and solve for the other variable.

Example 1 (Graphing)

Solve the system by graphing:
y=2x+1y=-x+4

  • Graph both lines.
  • Identify point of intersection: (1,3).
  • Solution: (1,3).

Example 2 (Substitution)

Solve the system:
y=x+23x+2y=12

  • Substitute x+2 for y in second equation.
  • Solve for x: 3x+2(x+2)=12.
  • Simplify and solve: 3x+2x+4=12, 5x=8, x=8/5.
  • Find y: y=8/5+2.

Example 3 (Elimination)

Solve the system:
2x+y=7x-2y=6

  • Multiply second equation by 2: 2x-4y=12.
  • Subtract first equation from the new: 2x-4y-(2x+y)=12-7, simplifying to -5y=5.
  • Solve: y=-1.
  • Substitute into one original equation to find x.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Graphing is easiest for integer solutions; substitution or elimination more precise for fractions or decimals.
  • Check your solution by substituting values back into both original equations.
  • Choose substitution if a variable is already isolated; use elimination if variables can be easily canceled.

unit: Unit 8: Writing Equations of Lines (Point-Slope, Slope-Intercept, Standard Form)
description: Write linear equations from graphs, points, and slopes in point-slope, slope-intercept, and standard forms.
content:
Definitions

  • Slope-Intercept Form: y=mx+b , where m is slope and b is the y-intercept.
  • Point-Slope Form: y-y1 = m(x-x1) for a line of slope m through (x1,y1).
  • Standard Form: Ax+By=C with integers A, B, C, and often A≥0.
  • Slope (from two points): m= y2-y1 x2-x1 (undefined if denominator is 0).

Key Concepts

  • Use point-slope form when you know a point and slope; convert to slope-intercept or standard as needed.
  • To convert to standard form, move variables to the left and clear fractions.
  • Horizontal lines: y=k (slope 0). Vertical lines: x=c (undefined slope).

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. From slope and a point (x1,y1) and slope m:
    1. Write point-slope: y-y1 = m(x-x1) .
    2. Distribute and solve for y to get slope-intercept, or rearrange to standard form.
  2. From two points (x1,y1), (x2,y2):
    1. Compute slope m= y2-y1 x2-x1 .
    2. Use point-slope with either point, then simplify.
  3. Convert forms:
    • Slope-intercept → Standard: move terms and clear fractions so Ax+By=C with integers.
    • Point-slope → Slope-intercept: distribute m and solve for y.

Example 1 — From a point and slope

Through (2,-3) with slope m=4.

  • Point-slope: y--3=4(x-2) , i.e., y+3=4x-8 .
  • Slope-intercept: y=4x-11 .
  • Standard: 4x-y=11 .

Example 2 — From two points

Through (1,2) and (5,-6).

  1. Slope: m= -6-25-1 =-2 .
  2. Point-slope (using (1,2)): y-2=-2(x-1) .
  3. Slope-intercept: y=-2x+4 .
  4. Standard: 2x+y=4 .

Example 3 — From a graph (given intercept and slope)

Slope m=13 and y-intercept (0,-5).

  • Slope-intercept: y=13x-5 .
  • Standard (clear fractions): multiply both sides by 3 ⟶ x-3y=15 .

Special Cases

  • Horizontal line through (a,k): y=k (slope 0) → standard: 0x+y=k.
  • Vertical line through (c,b): x=c (undefined slope) → standard: x-c=0.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • When using point-slope, substitute carefully: negatives inside (x-x1) become addition if x1 is negative.
  • Always simplify to remove double signs and reduce fractions.
  • For standard form, clear fractions and prefer A≥0.
  • Check with a point from the problem to verify your equation.

unit: Unit 9: Linear Inequalities and Systems of Inequalities
description: Graph and solve linear inequalities and systems of inequalities and interpret feasible regions.
content:
Definitions

  • Linear Inequality: A comparison using symbols <, >, ≤, or ≥ between linear expressions.
  • Solution of an Inequality: Any value that makes the inequality true.
  • System of Linear Inequalities: Two or more linear inequalities in the same variables; the solution set is their intersection.

Key Concepts

  • Solving steps mirror equations; but if you multiply or divide by a negative, reverse the inequality sign.
  • Graphing an inequality shades a half-plane: the boundary line is solid for ≤ or ≥, dashed for < or >.
  • For systems, the feasible region is where all individual shadings overlap.

Step-by-Step Procedures

  • Solving Linear Inequalities:
    1. Simplify both sides (distribute, combine like terms).
    2. Isolate the variable using inverse operations.
    3. If you multiply or divide by a negative, reverse the inequality symbol.
  • Graphing a Single Linear Inequality:
    1. Rewrite its boundary in slope-intercept form y=mx+b (or the equivalent line).
    2. Draw the boundary line: solid for ≤/≥, dashed for </>.
    3. Use a test point (e.g., (0,0)) to decide which side to shade.
  • Solving a System:
    1. Graph each inequality on the same axes with its correct boundary style.
    2. Shade the correct side for each; the overlap is the solution set.

Example 1 — Solve and graph

Inequality: 2x-3y<6

  1. Boundary line: 2x-3y=6. Intercepts: (3,0) and (0,-2).
  2. Line style: dashed (strict <).
  3. Test point: (0,0): 2⁢0-3⁢0<6 is true, so shade the side containing the origin.

Example 2 — Graph the system

y≤2x+3y>-x+1

  • Boundary lines: solid for ≤, dashed for >.
  • Shade at or below the first line (y≤2x+3) and above the second (y>-x+1).
  • The feasible region is the overlap of these two shadings.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative.
  • Use a simple test point to confirm shading direction.
  • Solid lines include the boundary (≤, ≥); dashed lines exclude it (<, >).
  • If no overlap exists in a system, there is no solution.

description: Describe and apply translations, reflections, and vertical/horizontal stretches and compressions of y = ax^2 in vertex form y = a(x − h)^2 + k; interpret how a, h, and k affect the graph.
content:
Definitions

  • Quadratic Function: A function in the form f(x)=ax2+bx+c , where a≠0.
  • Parent Function: The simplest quadratic function, f(x)=x2 , whose graph is a parabola with vertex at the origin.
  • Transformation: A change in position, shape, or orientation of a graph including translations, reflections, stretches, and compressions.

Key Concepts

  • The general vertex form of a quadratic is f(x)=a(x-h)2+k , where:
    • h and k represent horizontal and vertical translations.
    • a determines vertical stretch/compression and reflection.
  • Translation: Moves the graph without changing its shape.
    • Left/Right: change h
    • Up/Down: change k
  • Reflection: Occurs across the x-axis when a<0 (the parabola opens downward).
  • Vertical Stretch/Compression: Controlled by a:
    • If |a|>1 → parabola becomes narrower (stretched).
    • If 0<|a|<1 → parabola becomes wider (compressed).

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Identify transformations from vertex form y=a(x-h)2+k :
    • Start with the parent function y=x2.
    • Shift right if h>0, left if h<0.
    • Shift up if k>0, down if k<0.
    • Reflect across x-axis if a<0.
    • Apply stretch/compression based on |a|.
  2. Graphing Procedure
    1. Plot the vertex at (h,k).
    2. Determine direction of opening (up/down).
    3. Plot one point to the right of the vertex and use symmetry to find a matching point on the left.
    4. Sketch the parabola smoothly through all points.

Example 1 — Translation

Given y=(x-3)2+2

  • Shift right 3 units, up 2 units.
  • Vertex: (3, 2), opens upward.

Example 2 — Reflection and Stretch

Given y=-2(x+1)2

  • Reflection across x-axis (because coefficient is negative).
  • Vertical stretch by factor of 2 (narrower parabola).
  • Shift left 1 unit; vertex (-1, 0).

Example 3 — Compression and Downward Shift

Given y=12x2-4

  • Wider parabola (compressed by ½).
  • Shifted down 4 units; vertex (0, -4).

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Signs inside parentheses indicate the opposite direction of translation (e.g., (x - 3) → right 3).
  • The coefficient of x² (a) controls both direction and shape.
  • Always graph vertex first, then use symmetry to find additional points.
  • Combine transformations in order: stretch/reflect first, then translate.

description: Identify vertex, axis of symmetry, direction of opening, intercepts, domain, range, and maximum/minimum; relate features to parameters in standard and vertex forms and analyze average rate of change.
content:
Definitions

  • Quadratic Function: A function that can be written in standard form f(x)=ax2+bx+c with a≠0.
  • Vertex: The highest or lowest point of the parabola; in vertex form f(x)=a(x-h)2+k the vertex is (h,k).
  • Axis of Symmetry: Vertical line through the vertex that splits the parabola into mirror images; in standard form it is x=-b2a .
  • Opening/Direction: If a>0 the parabola opens up (minimum); if a<0 it opens down (maximum).
  • Intercepts: y-intercept at (0,c); x-intercepts (zeros) are solutions to f(x)=0.
  • Discriminant: D=b2-4ac indicates number of real zeros.

Key Concepts

  • From standard form, the axis is x=-b2a; plug this x-value into f(x) to get the vertex.
  • Vertex form f(x)=a(x-h)2+k reveals vertex and direction immediately; the axis is x=h.
  • If D>0: two real zeros; D=0: one real zero (tangent); D<0: no real zeros.
  • Vertical stretch/compression: larger |a| makes the parabola narrower; smaller makes it wider.

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. From standard form f(x)=ax2+bx+c:
    1. Axis: x=-b2a.
    2. Vertex: evaluate f at the axis.
    3. Opening: sign of a; y-intercept: c.
    4. Zeros: factor, complete the square, or quadratic formula using D.
  2. From vertex form f(x)=a(x-h)2+k:
    1. Vertex: (h,k); axis: x=h.
    2. Opening and width from a; y-intercept by evaluating at x=0.

Example 1 — Standard form

Given f(x)=x2-4x+3

  • Axis: x=42⁢1=2.
  • Vertex: (2,f(2)) with f(2)=22-8+3=-1; vertex (2,-1).
  • Opening: up ( a=1>0). y-intercept: c=3.
  • Zeros (factor): (x-1)(x-3)=0 ⟶ x=1, x=3.

Example 2 — Vertex form

Given g(x)=-2(x+1)2+5

  • Vertex: (-1,5); axis: x=-1.
  • Opening: down ( a=-2), so vertex is a maximum of 5.
  • y-intercept: evaluate at x=0: g(0)=-2(1)2+5=3.

Example 3 — Discriminant and zeros

Given h(x)=2x2+3x+5

  • Discriminant: D=32-4⁢2⁢5=9-40=-31 → no real zeros.
  • Parabola lies entirely above the x-axis if the vertex y-value is positive and a>0; compute vertex if needed to justify.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Use the axis formula first from standard form; it prevents algebra slips when completing the square.
  • Remember: sign of a decides min vs. max.
  • Check intercepts carefully; not all quadratics cross the x-axis.
  • When converting to vertex form, complete the square accurately and keep the balance inside/outside the parentheses.

unit: Unit 12: Graphing Quadratic Functions (Standard, Vertex, and Intercept Forms)
description: Graph quadratics given in standard ax^2 + bx + c, vertex a(x − h)^2 + k, and intercept a(x − p)(x − q) forms; convert between forms and use key features to sketch accurate graphs.
content:
Definitions

  • Standard Form: y=ax2+bx+c — used to find the vertex using the axis of symmetry and evaluate for the y-value.
  • Vertex Form: y=a(x-h)2+k — reveals the vertex (h,k) directly.
  • Intercept Form (Factored Form): y=a(x-r_1)(x-r_2) — shows x-intercepts (zeros) directly at r_1 and r_2.
  • Axis of Symmetry: x=-b2a, divides the parabola symmetrically.
  • Direction: If a>0 the parabola opens upward; if a<0, downward.

Key Concepts

  • Each form of a quadratic reveals different key features: vertex, intercepts, and symmetry.
  • All graphs are parabolas, which are symmetric about their axis.
  • Changing a changes the width and direction; changing h or k shifts the graph horizontally or vertically.

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Graphing from Standard Form
    1. Find axis: x=-b2a.
    2. Substitute to find vertex.
    3. Plot vertex and y-intercept.
    4. Find a symmetric point across the axis.
    5. Sketch the parabola using direction of opening.
  2. Graphing from Vertex Form
    1. Identify vertex (h,k).
    2. Plot vertex and axis x=h.
    3. Choose x-values around h to find symmetric points.
    4. Plot points and draw the parabola.
  3. Graphing from Intercept Form
    1. Identify zeros r_1 and r_2.
    2. Find the axis midpoint: x=r_1+r_22.
    3. Substitute the midpoint to get vertex y-value.
    4. Plot intercepts, vertex, and sketch the parabola.

Example 1 — Standard Form

Graph y=x2-4x+1

  • Axis: x=2.
  • Vertex: (2,y) → y=22-8+1=-3.
  • Vertex: (2, -3), opens up.
  • y-intercept: (0, 1). Symmetric point: (4, 1).

Example 2 — Vertex Form

Graph y=-2(x-3)2+4

  • Vertex: (3, 4).
  • Opens down ( a<0).
  • Axis: x=3.
  • Choose x-values 2 and 4 to find symmetric points, then plot and connect.

Example 3 — Intercept Form

Graph y=x(x-6)

  • x-intercepts: (0, 0) and (6, 0).
  • Axis: midpoint between 0 and 6 → x=3.
  • Vertex: plug x=3 → y=3(3-6)=-9 → vertex (3, -9).
  • Plot (0,0), (6,0), (3,-9); opens upward.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Check the form of the equation before graphing—it determines the quickest route to key features.
  • Always find and plot the vertex and axis first.
  • Use symmetry to plot matching points efficiently.
  • Remember that negative a flips the parabola vertically.

unit: Unit 13: Focus and Directrix of a Parabola
description: Define a parabola using focus and directrix; derive and use (x − h)^2 = 4p(y − k) and (y − k)^2 = 4p(x − h); find focus, directrix, and parameter p; graph parabolas from geometric data.
content:
Definitions

  • Parabola (focus–directrix definition): The set of all points equidistant from a fixed point (the focus) and a fixed line (the directrix).
  • Vertex: The midpoint (along the axis of symmetry) between the focus and the directrix; the point where the parabola turns.
  • Axis of Symmetry: The line through the vertex and focus that splits the parabola into mirror images.
  • Focal Length (often p): The directed distance from the vertex to the focus (and to the directrix).

Key Forms & Relationships

  • Vertical orientation (opens up/down):
    • Standard (focus–directrix) form: (x-h)2 = 4p(y-k) ; vertex (h,k), axis x=h.
    • Vertex form: y=a (x-h)2 +k with p=14a. Focus: (h,k+p); Directrix: y=k-p.
  • Horizontal orientation (opens right/left):
    • Standard form: (y-k)2 = 4p(x-h) ; vertex (h,k), axis y=k.
    • Equivalent vertex form: x=a (y-k)2 +h with p=14a. Focus: (h+p,k); Directrix: x=h-p.
  • Direction of opening: For vertical form, p>0 (or a>0) opens up; p<0 (or a<0) opens down. Analogous for horizontal (right/left).

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Given vertex form (vertical) y=a (x-h)2 +k:
    1. Compute p=14a.
    2. Focus (h,k+p); Directrix y=k-p; Axis x=h.
  2. Given standard focus–directrix form (x-h)2=4p(y-k) (vertical) or (y-k)2=4p(x-h) (horizontal):
    1. Vertex is (h,k); identify p from the coefficient.
    2. Place focus and directrix using the rules above.

Example 1 — From vertex form (vertical)

Given y=18 (x-2)2 +3

  • a=18 so p=14⁢18=2.
  • Focus: (2,3+2)=(2,5); Directrix: y=3-2=1.
  • Axis: x=2; opens up (since a>0).

Example 2 — From standard form (vertical, opens down)

Given (x+4)2 =-12(y-1)

  • Here 4p=-12 so p=-3; vertex (-4,1).
  • Focus: (-4,1+-3)=(-4,-2); Directrix: y=1--3=4.
  • Opens downward because p<0 (equivalently, the right side coefficient is negative).

Example 3 — Horizontal orientation

Given (y-2)2 =8(x-1)

  • 4p=8 so p=2; vertex (1,2).
  • Focus: (1+2,2)=(3,2); Directrix: x=1-2=-1.
  • Opens to the right since p>0.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Relate a and p with p=14a to move between vertex and focus–directrix perspectives.
  • Watch signs: a negative p (or a) flips the opening direction.
  • Axis is always halfway between focus and directrix and passes through the vertex.
  • When completing the square to reach vertex form, keep track of horizontal/vertical shifts (h,k) correctly before applying focus/directrix formulas.

description: Model real-world situations using quadratic functions (e.g., projectile motion, area optimization); interpret coefficients and vertex; select appropriate form and use technology for regression when needed.
content:
Definitions

  • Quadratic Model: An equation of the form y=ax2+bx+c used to represent real-world phenomena involving parabolic relationships.
  • Vertex: The point (h,k) where a parabola attains its maximum or minimum.

Key Concepts

  • Many real-world problems—such as the motion of projectiles, maximizing profit, or finding areas—can be modeled using quadratic equations.
  • The maximum or minimum value of the situation may correspond to the vertex of the quadratic model.
  • When modeling with a quadratic, identify the variable (often time, height, area, or quantity) and interpret the parameters (a, b, c) in context.

Step-by-Step Procedure

  1. Define all variables. Translate the real-world situation into a quadratic equation.
  2. Set up the equation, writing expressions for unknowns if necessary.
  3. Find the vertex if you need to determine a maximum or minimum.
  4. Solve for zeros if you need to determine a time, distance, or quantity.
  5. Interpret your solution in the context of the original problem.

Example 1

Projectile Motion: The height (in meters) of a ball thrown upward is modeled by h=-5t2+20t+3, where t is time in seconds.

  • Maximum height: Find the vertex using t=-b2a; here, a=-5, b=20 so t=-202∗-5 = 2 seconds.
  • Plug back to find the maximum height: h=-5(22)+20∗2+3=-20+40+3=23. So, the ball reaches a maximum height of 23 meters.

Example 2

Optimizing Profit: A company models profit by P=-2x2+40x+100 where x is thousands of items sold.

  • Find number of items for maximum profit: Vertex at x=-b2a = -402∗-2 = 10.
  • Maximum profit: P=-2(102)+40∗10+100=-200+400+100=300 (in thousands).

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Carefully define all variables in the context of the problem.
  • Check if a quadratic model is appropriate—look for words like "maximum," "minimum," or "squared" relationships.
  • Always interpret the answer in context—avoid giving meaningless negative times or quantities.

unit: Unit 15: Solving Quadratic Equations (By Graphing, Factoring, Completing the Square, Quadratic Formula)
description: Solve quadratic equations using graphing, factoring, completing the square, and the quadratic formula; justify steps, choose efficient methods, and verify solutions (including complex solutions).
content:
Definitions

  • Quadratic Equation: An equation of the form ax2+bx+c=0 with a≠0.
  • Solutions / Roots / Zeros: Values of x that satisfy the equation.
  • Discriminant: D=b2-4ac determines the number and type of solutions.

Key Concepts

  • Graphing: Solve by finding x-intercepts of y=ax2+bx+c (if they exist).
  • Factoring: Rewrite as a product and use the zero-product property.
  • Completing the Square: Convert to a perfect square form to solve.
  • Quadratic Formula: Always works: x= -b±b2-4ac 2a
  • Using the Discriminant: If D>0 → two real solutions; D=0 → one real solution (double root); D<0 → no real solutions (complex conjugates).

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. By Graphing
    1. Graph y=ax2+bx+c.
    2. Identify x-intercepts (if any); those x-values are the solutions.
